works with any device that has a Linux driver and a devicetree binding. It

The workfile is the devicetree overlay that Analog Attach creates and edits.
Which file it is, is decided by the `workfile` setting
(Configuration file).

1. The `workfile` setting names the file. Set it with
  `analog-attach config workfile <name>` or when answering the questions of
  a bare `analog-attach` run.
2. `analog-attach init` checks that the Linux kernel tree and the base
  devicetree are configured and load correctly. It does not read or v

- Every command that changes the workfile rewrites the **whole file**, printed
  from the parsed tree and indented with tabs.
- **Comments and the original layout are not kept.** A comment you add by hand
  is dropped the next time a command writes the file.
- The workfile can’t contain preprocessor

to the whole file on every write, whatever syntax the file was in.

`list property` lists the properties the node’s binding defines, with their
types. `set` marks those the node has, `required` those it must have:

```text
$ analog-attach list property accel
compatible        (set, required)  enum("adi,adxl346", "adi,adxl345" | adi,adxl345 | adi,adxl375)
reg

`list value` lists the values that fit, each ready to pass to `update`. For
a reference such as `interrupt-parent`, those are the nodes of the base and
the overlay that can be named:

```text
$ analog-attach list value accel interrupt-parent
gpio   gpio — interrupt controller, #interrupt-cells = <2>

`update <node> <property> <value>...` sets a property, replacing the value it
had. The ADXL345’s interrupt pin is on GPIO 27, rising edge:

```text
$ analog-attach update accel interrupt-parent gpio
Set interrupt-parent on accel
$ analog-attach update accel interrupts 27 IRQ_TYPE_EDGE_RISING
Set int

The values after the property name are joined with spaces, so
`update accel interrupts 27 1` and `update accel interrupts "27 1"` are the
same.
|Value|Example|Written as|
|Numbers, decimal or hexadecimal|`update accel reg 0x1d`|`reg = <0x1d>;`|
|Several cells|`update accel interrupts 27 1`|`interrup

`update` checks each value against the node’s binding:

- A value that can’t be built is refused, and nothing is written:
  $ analog-attach update accel interrupts 27 RISING

- A value the binding doesn’t allow is written,

Setting `reg` also renames the node, so that its unit address matches:

```text
$ analog-attach update accel reg 0x53
Set reg on accel; renamed to adxl345@53
```

Every command can run unattended: in a shell script, a Makefile, a CI job or an
AI agent. This page shows how to get machine-readable answers and how to tell
success from failure. The format itself is in JSON protocol.

A command only asks questions when both its standard input and its standard
output are a terminal, and `--json` isn’t given. Piped, redirected or with

board runs. Analog Attach takes two things from it: the *bindings*, YAML files
in `Documentation/devicetree/bindings/` that say which properties each
device takes, and the includes the devicetrees use.

The *workfile* is the devicetree overlay (a `.dtso` file) that you build up
with `add` and `update`. The `workfile` setting names it, and
`analog-attach init` creates it. See Workfile.

*properties*. A device node sits under the bus

`--json` can be anywhere on the command line before a `--`:
`analog-attach --json read accel` and `analog-attach read accel --json` are
the same. In JSON mode the CLI never asks a question.

|Stream|What it gets|
|Standard output|At most one line: the JSON answer. Nothing else.|
|Standard error|Notes and warnings (the bus `add` picked, an address clash, a cache out of date), the progress of long steps, the output of the `build` and `deploy` commands, and input errors. This is free text:

|Status|When|Standard output|
|0|The command answered: a success, a refusal, or a configuration error. Also `--help` and `--version`.|The JSON answer (`--help` and `--version` print text).|
|1|The command failed without answering (an unexpected error).|Nothing, or what the command wrote before faili

Analog Attach can be driven by an AI agent. The agent runs the same
`analog-attach` commands you would, reads their `--json` answers, and asks
you what only you know: which part you have and how it is wired. The skill is
written and tested for **Claude Code**; it can also be installed for Codex CLI

A *skill* is a set of instructions the agent loads when a task needs it: here,
how to use the CLI, in which order, and what to ask the user. The package
ships one skill for each backend; in v0.2.0 that is `analog-attach-linux`.

```bash
analog-attach skill install analog-attach-linux
```

The GUI is a page in your browser, served by the `analog-attach` CLI on your
own machine. Each GUI belongs to one project: the folder you start it in.

1. Open a terminal in the project folder. For a new project, make an empty
  folder first:
  mkdir ~/rpi-adxl345
  cd ~/rpi-adxl345
2. Run:
  analog-attach gui
  The CLI prints where the page is, then opens it in your default browser:
  analog-attach GUI on http://127.0.0.1:5177  (project: /home/use

The page is served on `127.0.0.1` only, so only your own machine can reach
it. Without `--port`, the GUI uses port 5177. If 5177 is taken (for example,
by another open GUI), it takes the first free port of the 20 after it, else any
free port. The URL printed always tells you which.
